species.nativeRange: Eastern Siberia, NE Mongolia, NE China, Korean peninsula
species.whyCommon: Likely among the most numerous mature trees on Earth; dominates vast East Siberian larch taiga on permafrost.

idFeatures.bark: Young bark smooth gray-brown; older trunks scaly and reddish-brown with shallow furrows.
idFeatures.needles: Deciduous soft needles 2–3 cm in tufts on short shoots; bright green, then yellow-orange before falling.
idFeatures.cones: Small erect ovoid cones 1–2 cm with 15–25 moderately reflexed scales; old dull-gray cones persist for years.
idFeatures.habit: Medium tree 10–30 m with a broad-conic crown of mostly level branches; often open fire-shaped stands on permafrost.

species.nativeRange: Western and central Siberia west of the Yenisei
species.whyCommon: Principal larch of western Siberia; together with L. gmelinii it forms the world's most extensive larch forests.

idFeatures.bark: Thick, furrowed, cinnamon to gray-brown bark flaking in plates.
idFeatures.needles: Deciduous needles in tufts of 20–40 on spur shoots, slightly longer and paler than Dahurian larch.
idFeatures.cones: Erect cones 2.5–4.5 cm, larger than Dahurian larch, with more spreading scales.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled tree to 40 m; hybridizes with L. gmelinii along the Yenisei (L. × czekanowskii).

species.nativeRange: Eurasia from Spain and Scotland to eastern Siberia
species.whyCommon: World's most widespread pine and second-most widespread conifer after common juniper; over 28 million ha in Europe alone.

idFeatures.bark: Upper trunk distinctive orange-red and flaky; lower trunk thick, gray-brown, and plated.
idFeatures.needles: Blue-green needles in pairs, 2.5–5 cm, slightly twisted, with a persistent basal sheath.
idFeatures.cones: Small pointed ovoid cones 3–7.5 cm, gray-brown, with a small prickle on the umbo.
idFeatures.habit: Long, often bare, straight trunk topped by a rounded or flat-topped crown.

species.nativeRange: Northern and central Europe; widely planted beyond
species.whyCommon: Europe's most important commercial conifer and a core boreal dominant; among the most frequent trees on European forest plots.

idFeatures.bark: Thin reddish-brown bark becoming gray-brown and flaky in small plates.
idFeatures.needles: Four-sided, stiff, dark-green needles 1–2.5 cm on peg-like sterigmata; they roll easily between fingers.
idFeatures.cones: Large hanging cylindrical cones 9–17 cm with thin diamond-shaped, irregularly toothed scales (contrast Sitka's papery scales and Siberian spruce's rounded scales).
idFeatures.habit: Tall spire with drooping branchlets; often in dense even-aged stands.

species.nativeRange: Northeastern Europe to Siberia and northern Mongolia
species.whyCommon: Second major Eurasian spruce; dominates dark taiga east of the Urals and hybridizes with Norway spruce (Picea × fennica).

idFeatures.bark: Thin gray-brown flaky bark similar to Norway spruce.
idFeatures.needles: Four-sided green needles on woody pegs, typically slightly blunter than Norway spruce.
idFeatures.cones: Hanging cones 5–8 cm with smoothly rounded (not toothed) seed-scale margins — the key split from Norway spruce.
idFeatures.habit: Narrow-crowned dark-taiga tree, often mixed with Siberian fir and Siberian pine.

species.biome: North American boreal bog and upland
species.nativeRange: Alaska and Canada to the northern Great Lakes and Northeast US
species.whyCommon: Nearly ubiquitous dominant of North American boreal peatlands and a major component of spruce-fir ecosystems.

idFeatures.bark: Thin, scaly, gray-brown bark; inner bark often olive.
idFeatures.needles: Short (0.6–1.5 cm), blunt, four-sided, bluish-green needles densely clothing twigs.
idFeatures.cones: Small egg-shaped cones 1.5–3.5 cm that persist for years in clusters near the crown (semi-serotinous).
idFeatures.habit: Often skinny and spire-like with a club-shaped top; common in bogs. Contrast white spruce: longer needles and cones that drop.

species.biome: North American boreal and montane forest
species.nativeRange: Alaska across Canada to northern US
species.whyCommon: Codominant of North American boreal forest on better-drained sites, with a huge range from treeline to mixedwood.

idFeatures.bark: Thin ash-brown scaly plates; inner bark silvery.
idFeatures.needles: Four-sided, 1.2–2.4 cm, bluish-green; crushed needles smell resinous, not the skunky odor of black spruce.
idFeatures.cones: Cylindrical hanging cones 3–7 cm that fall soon after seed release.
idFeatures.habit: Conical crown, often denser than black spruce; upland and river-terrace sites.

species.nativeRange: Urals through western and central Siberia to Mongolia
species.whyCommon: A main dark-taiga five-needle pine of Siberia, often codominant with spruce and fir over tens of millions of hectares.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, becoming thick and furrowed with reddish plates.
idFeatures.needles: Five needles per fascicle, 6–11 cm, dark green, triangular in cross-section (white-pine group).
idFeatures.cones: Large egg-shaped cones 5–13 cm that do not open fully on the tree; seeds are wingless cedar nuts.
idFeatures.habit: Broad-crowned tree to 40 m in humid dark taiga.

species.nativeRange: NE European Russia through Siberia to NE China
species.whyCommon: Principal fir of the Siberian dark taiga; Abies forests occupy over 10 million ha in western Siberia alone.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth gray with resin blisters on young trunks; later shallowly fissured.
idFeatures.needles: Flat, notched, aromatic needles 1.5–3 cm with two white stomatal bands below; attached by a disk, not pegs.
idFeatures.cones: Upright cylindrical cones 5–9 cm that disintegrate on the tree, leaving a central spike.
idFeatures.habit: Narrow spire; shade-tolerant late-successional tree of humid taiga.

species.nativeRange: Europe and northern Asia
species.whyCommon: Most widespread Eurasian birch; a post-fire pioneer across taiga and temperate Europe and among the most frequent trees on European plots.

idFeatures.bark: White, peeling in papery sheets with black diamond-shaped fissures at the base; smoother and whiter than downy birch.
idFeatures.leaves: Triangular-ovate with a long-pointed tip and double-toothed margin; hairless, on pendulous twigs.
idFeatures.flowers: Dangling yellow male catkins in spring; female catkins become pendulous fruiting cylinders.
idFeatures.habit: Graceful tree with drooping, warty (not hairy) branchlets — contrast downy birch.

species.nativeRange: Northern Europe and northern Asia
species.whyCommon: The more northerly Eurasian birch; dominates wetter, colder sites and treeline birch woods, and is among Europe's most frequent trees.

idFeatures.bark: Dull gray-white, less peeling and less black-diamond-marked than silver birch.
idFeatures.leaves: More rounded ovate blade with a short point; young shoots downy, not warty.
idFeatures.flowers: Catkins similar to silver birch; use hairy twigs as the split.
idFeatures.habit: Less pendulous crown; occupies bogs and high latitudes where silver birch drops out.

species.nativeRange: Europe and temperate Asia
species.whyCommon: Circumboreal aspen of Eurasia; a fire-pioneer that clones across taiga and temperate woodland with birch.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth greenish-gray becoming darker and furrowed at the base; lenticels diamond-shaped.
idFeatures.leaves: Round to ovate with a wavy-toothed margin and a flattened petiole that makes the blade tremble.
idFeatures.flowers: Dioecious dangling catkins before leaf-out.
idFeatures.habit: Clonal groves of straight gray trunks; sister species of quaking aspen.

species.nativeRange: Western North America from Alaska to Baja California
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by stem count and volume; serotinous stands cover huge post-fire landscapes in the Interior West.

idFeatures.bark: Thin, scaly, gray-brown to orange-brown — much thinner than ponderosa.
idFeatures.needles: Two needles per fascicle, 3–7 cm, often twisted and yellow-green (ponderosa usually has three longer needles).
idFeatures.cones: Small, often serotinous, lopsided cones 3–6 cm with sharp prickles; persist closed until fire.
idFeatures.habit: Straight, slender lodgepole with a narrow crown in dense even-aged stands.

species.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern US
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by stem count; a spruce-fir dominant of eastern boreal forests and a major Christmas-tree species.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth gray with prominent resin blisters on young trees; later shallowly scaly.
idFeatures.needles: Flat, blunt or notched, 1.5–3 cm, dark green above with two white bands below; balsam-scented.
idFeatures.cones: Upright dark-purple cones 4–8 cm that shatter on the tree.
idFeatures.habit: Spire-shaped; needles attached by a disk, not pegs (unlike spruce).

species.nativeRange: Alps, Carpathians, and Sudetes; widely planted in Europe
species.whyCommon: Native Alpine dominant and one of Europe's most planted deciduous conifers; frequent on European forest plots.

idFeatures.bark: Pinkish-brown, becoming deeply furrowed into scaly plates.
idFeatures.needles: Deciduous tufts of 30–40 soft needles 2–4 cm; brilliant yellow in autumn.
idFeatures.cones: Erect ovoid cones 2–5 cm with straight (not strongly reflexed) scales.
idFeatures.habit: Open, irregular crown; widely used in forestry.

species.biome: Pacific temperate rainforest; also North Sea plantations
species.nativeRange: Pacific coast from Alaska to northern California; extensively planted in UK and Ireland
species.whyCommon: Tallest spruce and a hyperdominant of Pacific Northwest rainforests; the UK's most planted commercial conifer; a quiz lookalike of Norway spruce.

idFeatures.bark: Thin, purplish-gray, peeling in large papery plates.
idFeatures.needles: Flattened (not 4-sided), very sharp, blue-green with two white stomatal bands; painful to grasp.
idFeatures.cones: Hanging pale-brown cones 5–10 cm with thin, wavy, papery, irregularly toothed scales.
idFeatures.habit: Massive coastal tree with hanging branchlets; in Europe, dense plantation spires.

plates.commonsTitle: File:Sitka Spruce (Picea sitchensis) foliage, Sitka National Historical Park (bf83265e-1dd8-b71c-0715-310543ca4965).jpg

species.biome: southeastern US pine plantation and coastal plain
species.nativeRange: Southeastern United States
species.whyCommon: Most commonly planted US tree and second by stem count (about 19 billion in early-2000s FIA); backbone of the southern pine estate.

idFeatures.bark: Thick reddish-brown plates with deep furrows on mature trees.
idFeatures.needles: Usually three (sometimes two) needles per fascicle, 12–22 cm, yellowish-green, fairly stiff.
idFeatures.cones: Ovoid cones 6–12 cm with sharp prickles on the umbos.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled plantation pine of the southern coastal plain; contrast slash pine's longer shinier needles.

species.nativeRange: Eastern North America
species.whyCommon: Most common tree in US forests by stem count (about 22 billion; ~7.6% of all US trees in early-2000s FIA).

idFeatures.bark: Smooth light gray when young, becoming darker and shaggy-plated; not the deeply furrowed elephant-hide of sugar maple.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, 3–5 palmate lobes with V-shaped sinuses and serrated margins; petiole often red.
idFeatures.flowers: Small red clusters before leaves in early spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Paired red samaras that ripen in late spring (sugar maple samaras ripen in autumn).

species.nativeRange: Alaska and Canada to Mexico in the Rockies
species.whyCommon: Most widely distributed tree in North America; among the top US species by stem count, forming the largest known clonal organisms.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth pale green-white to cream with black knots; does not peel like birch.
idFeatures.leaves: Round, finely toothed, with a flattened petiole that makes them quake; gold in autumn.
idFeatures.flowers: Dioecious catkins before leaf-out.
idFeatures.habit: Clonal groves of identical trunks; often the first tree after fire in the Rockies.

species.biome: Pacific Northwest and Rocky Mountain temperate forest
species.nativeRange: Western North America
species.whyCommon: Most common US tree by live volume (about 13% of national volume); a regional hyperdominant and widely planted timber species.

idFeatures.bark: Young bark smooth with resin blisters; mature bark very thick, corky, and deeply furrowed into reddish-brown ridges.
idFeatures.needles: Soft, flat needles 2–4 cm attached singly by a small stalk (not a disk like true firs or pegs like spruce); citrus-resin scent.
idFeatures.cones: Hanging cones 5–10 cm with distinctive three-pointed bracts protruding beyond the scales (mouse tails).
idFeatures.habit: Huge straight-boled tree; not a true fir (Abies).

species.biome: dry montane and interior West pine forest
species.nativeRange: Western North America
species.whyCommon: Third US tree by live volume; the characteristic yellow pine of dry western forests and a lookalike contrast to lodgepole.

idFeatures.bark: Mature bark in large jigsaw plates of yellow-orange to cinnamon that smell of vanilla or butterscotch.
idFeatures.needles: Usually three long needles 12–20 cm in a fascicle, stiff, yellow-green.
idFeatures.cones: Ovoid cones 8–15 cm with out-turned prickles; much larger than lodgepole cones.
idFeatures.habit: Open-grown, large-crowned pine of fire-maintained savannas.

species.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern and midwestern US
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by stems and volume; the maple-syrup tree and a northern-hardwoods dominant, a lookalike of red maple.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, becoming deeply furrowed into long plated ridges (elephant hide).
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, 5-lobed with U-shaped sinuses and mostly entire lobe margins (red maple has V-sinuses and teeth).
idFeatures.fruit: U-shaped paired samaras ripening in autumn.
idFeatures.habit: Shade-tolerant canopy tree with spectacular orange-red fall color.

species.biome: eastern North American temperate deciduous forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern United States
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by volume and a white-oak-group dominant; a core quiz species versus the red-oak group.

idFeatures.bark: Light gray, scaly, and flaky in long plates.
idFeatures.leaves: Obovate with 7–9 rounded lobes and no bristle tips (white-oak group); pale below.
idFeatures.fruit: Acorns with a shallow bumpy cup covering about one-quarter of a sweet nut; mature in one season.
idFeatures.habit: Broad-crowned, long-lived canopy oak.

species.biome: eastern North American temperate deciduous forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern North America
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by volume; the widespread red-oak-group species taught against white oak.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray with shiny vertical ski-track ridges on mature trunks.
idFeatures.leaves: 7–11 pointed lobes each ending in a bristle tip (red-oak group).
idFeatures.fruit: Large acorns with a shallow saucer cup; bitter, mature in two seasons.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled timber oak, also widely planted in Europe.

species.biome: southeastern US bottomland and mixed forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern US, Mexico, and Central America
species.whyCommon: Third most numerous US tree (about 13 billion stems in early-2000s FIA); a southern bottomland associate of loblolly pine.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, deeply furrowed into narrow ridges; twigs often winged with corky ridges.
idFeatures.leaves: Star-shaped, palmately 5–7 lobed, finely toothed; brilliant red-purple-gold in fall.
idFeatures.fruit: Woody spherical gumball multiple capsules hanging on long stalks, persisting into winter.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled deciduous tree of moist lowlands and streets.

species.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern US Appalachians
species.whyCommon: Shade-tolerant late-successional dominant of eastern ravines and mixed forests; a lookalike of western hemlock.

idFeatures.bark: Reddish-brown, becoming deeply furrowed; inner bark cinnamon.
idFeatures.needles: Short (1–2 cm) flat needles of uneven length, dark green above with two white bands below.
idFeatures.cones: Small hanging ovoid cones 1.5–2.5 cm (smaller than western hemlock).
idFeatures.habit: Feathery, drooping leader; deep shade understory to canopy.

species.nativeRange: Pacific coast from Alaska to California, inland to the northern Rockies
species.whyCommon: Among the top US trees by volume; a hyperdominant of Pacific Northwest rainforests with Douglas-fir and Sitka spruce.

idFeatures.bark: Thin russet-brown bark, becoming furrowed on old trees.
idFeatures.needles: Distinctly unequal in length (hence heterophylla), flat, glossy, two white bands below.
idFeatures.cones: Hanging cones 2–8 cm, larger than eastern hemlock.
idFeatures.habit: Drooping terminal leader is diagnostic; often the climax species of coastal rainforest.

species.biome: eastern North American mixed and northern forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern Canada and northeastern and Great Lakes US
species.whyCommon: Historically the great timber pine of eastern North America; still a widespread five-needle pine of mixed forests and plantations.

idFeatures.bark: Young bark smooth and green-gray; mature bark dark gray with broad ridges.
idFeatures.needles: Five slender, blue-green, flexible needles 6–13 cm per fascicle (white-pine group).
idFeatures.cones: Long, slender, slightly curved cones 8–20 cm with thin unarmed scales.
idFeatures.habit: Horizontal whorled branches and a plume-like crown; contrast Scots pine's paired short needles.

plates.artist: Ana Raquel S. Hernandes from Sao Paulo, Brazil

species.biome: eastern North American mesic deciduous forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern United States
species.whyCommon: Among the top 10 US trees by volume; a fast-growing canopy dominant of rich Appalachian and midwestern forests.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, becoming deeply interlaced-furrowed on large trunks.
idFeatures.leaves: Unique four-lobed tulip or saddle-shaped leaves with a broad notch at the tip.
idFeatures.flowers: Large tuliplike green-yellow flowers with orange bases in late spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Upright cone-like aggregate of samaras that persist into winter.

species.biome: North American boreal and northern hardwoods
species.nativeRange: Alaska and Canada to northern US
species.whyCommon: The white-barked birch of boreal North America; a fire-pioneer across a huge range, often with aspen and spruce.

idFeatures.bark: Bright white, peeling in large papery sheets with dark lenticels; copper-brown on very young stems.
idFeatures.leaves: Ovate, double-toothed, 5–10 cm, paler below.
idFeatures.flowers: Dangling male catkins; smaller female catkins become cylindrical fruit.
idFeatures.habit: Often multi-stemmed groves after fire.

species.biome: eastern North American temperate deciduous forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern North America
species.whyCommon: Late-successional dominant of eastern mesic forests; a lookalike of European beech for a quiz.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth, thin, steel-gray even on old trees — a key field mark.
idFeatures.leaves: Ovate with straight parallel veins ending in sharp teeth; hold papery tan leaves in winter on young trees.
idFeatures.fruit: Spiny four-valved husk with two triangular nuts.
idFeatures.habit: Dense shade-tolerant canopy; contrast European beech's wavy, less sharply toothed margin.

species.biome: southeastern US coastal plain and subtropical plantation
species.nativeRange: Southeastern US coastal plain; planted in the subtropics
species.whyCommon: Major southern US timber pine and a widely planted subtropical pine in the global Pinus plantation estate.

idFeatures.bark: Orange-brown to purple-brown plates, thinner than mature loblolly.
idFeatures.needles: Two or three glossy dark-green needles 15–25 cm, longer and shinier than loblolly.
idFeatures.cones: Glossy caramel-brown, more globose cones 7–15 cm with short stout prickles.
idFeatures.habit: Coastal-plain and wet-flatwoods pine, also a global plantation species.

species.nativeRange: Eastern North America
species.whyCommon: Historically one of the most abundant eastern US hardwoods (now collapsing from emerald ash borer); retained as a common-tree ID target and lookalike of European ash.

idFeatures.bark: Gray with a tight diamond-ridge pattern.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, pinnately compound, usually 7 leaflets with whitish undersides.
idFeatures.fruit: Single-winged samaras in hanging clusters, the seed occupying the basal half.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled canopy tree; winter twigs with opposite horseshoe leaf scars.

species.nativeRange: Eastern North America to Arizona and Mexico; invasive in Europe
species.whyCommon: One of the most abundant eastern US trees and a major timber cherry; widely naturalized in Europe.

idFeatures.bark: Young bark smooth with lenticels; mature bark dark, scaly, burnt potato-chip plates.
idFeatures.leaves: Alternate, lanceolate, finely toothed, with orange-brown hairs along the midrib beneath.
idFeatures.flowers: Elongate white racemes in late spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Small black cherries in hanging clusters.

species.biome: eastern North American old-field, glade, and dry woodland
species.nativeRange: Eastern and central United States
species.whyCommon: The most widespread eastern US juniper; a hyper-abundant old-field invader of abandoned farmland and limestone glades.

idFeatures.bark: Fibrous, peeling in long reddish-brown strips.
idFeatures.needles: Scale-like adult leaves in opposite pairs; sharp awl-like juvenile leaves on young shoots.
idFeatures.cones: Dioecious; female berries are small glaucous-blue fleshy cones.
idFeatures.habit: Dense columnar to pyramidal evergreen; not a true cedar (Cedrus).

species.biome: southeastern US coastal plain and maritime forest
species.nativeRange: Southeastern US coastal plain
species.whyCommon: Iconic evergreen oak of the southern coastal plain and a dominant of maritime live-oak hammocks; widely planted as a street tree in the US South.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray-brown, thick, and deeply furrowed into blocky ridges.
idFeatures.leaves: Evergreen, leathery, oblong, with revolute margins and a pale hairy underside; no lobes.
idFeatures.fruit: Elongate dark acorns 1–2.5 cm, about one-third covered by a warty cup.
idFeatures.habit: Massive spreading crown, often with Spanish moss and low thick limbs.

species.nativeRange: Europe
species.whyCommon: Among Europe's most important and widespread broadleaves; would naturally dominate much of central Europe and is among the most frequent trees on European plots.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth, thin, silvery-gray even on old trees.
idFeatures.leaves: Ovate, wavy-margined with sparse teeth, 5–9 pairs of veins; silky when young.
idFeatures.fruit: Woody four-valved husk with two nuts (beechnuts).
idFeatures.habit: Dense shade-casting canopy; contrast American beech's more sharply toothed leaves.

species.nativeRange: Europe, Anatolia, Caucasus
species.whyCommon: Europe's classic oak and a continental dominant; among the most frequent trees on European plots, taught against sessile oak.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, deeply fissured into short ridges on old trees.
idFeatures.leaves: Short-stalked leaves with 3–6 rounded lobes and small ear-like auricles at the base.
idFeatures.fruit: Acorns on long stalks (peduncles) — the key contrast with sessile oak.
idFeatures.habit: Broad, often spreading crown of parkland and lowland forest.

species.nativeRange: Europe and Anatolia
species.whyCommon: Codominant European oak of uplands; paired with Q. robur as Europe's two main timber oaks.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, more regularly fissured than pedunculate oak.
idFeatures.leaves: On long petioles, lacking basal auricles; more regular lobes and a wedge-shaped base.
idFeatures.fruit: Acorns sessile (unstalked) in the leaf axils — the namesake contrast with Q. robur.
idFeatures.habit: Straighter bole, more upland and acid soils than pedunculate oak.

species.nativeRange: Europe and western Asia
species.whyCommon: A widespread European canopy hardwood of moist soils, now threatened by ash dieback but still among the continent's most encountered trees.

idFeatures.bark: Pale gray, becoming finely fissured; twigs with opposite black velvety buds (diagnostic).
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, pinnately compound, usually 9–13 leaflets (more than white ash).
idFeatures.fruit: Clusters of hanging single samaras (keys).
idFeatures.habit: Tall, light-demanding tree of rich moist soils.

species.nativeRange: Europe, western Asia, North Africa
species.whyCommon: The typical European streamside tree; among the most frequent species on European forest plots and a nitrogen-fixing wetland dominant.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray-brown, fissured into square plates; young twigs sticky (glutinosa).
idFeatures.leaves: Rounded with a notched (emarginate) tip and double-toothed margin; stay green late.
idFeatures.fruit: Woody persistent cones (strobiles) unlike birch catkins.
idFeatures.flowers: Early dangling male catkins; female catkins become the woody cones.

species.nativeRange: Europe and western Asia
species.whyCommon: A widespread understory-to-canopy tree of European oak-hornbeam forests, frequent on monitoring plots.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth steel-gray with a sinewy, muscular, fluted trunk.
idFeatures.leaves: Ovate, sharply double-toothed, with 10–15 pairs of impressed parallel veins.
idFeatures.fruit: Small nutlets each subtended by a 3-lobed leafy bract in hanging clusters.
idFeatures.habit: Often coppiced; dense hard wood.

species.biome: temperate European montane and planted woodland
species.nativeRange: Central and southern Europe and western Asia; widely naturalized
species.whyCommon: A major European maple of mountains and hedgerows, widely planted and naturalized; among frequent European plot species.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, flaking in irregular plates like a plane tree.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, 5-lobed, coarsely toothed; no milky sap in the petiole (unlike Norway maple).
idFeatures.fruit: Paired samaras at about 90 degrees (Norway maple is about 180 degrees).
idFeatures.habit: Large maple of parks, mountains, and disturbed woods.

species.biome: southern and western European woodland and orchard
species.nativeRange: Southern Europe and Asia Minor; long cultivated northward
species.whyCommon: A long-cultivated European nut tree and coppice species, frequent in Mediterranean and Atlantic woods.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown with spiral ridges on old trunks.
idFeatures.leaves: Long lanceolate, coarsely toothed, with parallel veins; 10–25 cm.
idFeatures.flowers: Long pale-yellow catkins in summer.
idFeatures.fruit: Spiny cupule enclosing 1–3 shiny brown edible nuts.

species.nativeRange: Europe and western Asia
species.whyCommon: A classic European forest and street lime; once a dominant of mixed oak-lime woods across the continent.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, smooth then finely fissured; young twigs reddish.
idFeatures.leaves: Heart-shaped, cordate, finely toothed, 3–8 cm, with rust-colored tufts in vein axils beneath.
idFeatures.flowers: Fragrant yellowish cymes hanging from a leafy bract in midsummer.
idFeatures.fruit: Small round nutlets with a thin shell.

species.nativeRange: Mountains of central and southern Europe
species.whyCommon: The principal true fir of European mountains and a major timber species; frequent on European plots.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth gray with resin blisters when young; later cracked into square plates.
idFeatures.needles: Flat, notched, in two ranks, dark green above with two silver stomatal bands below.
idFeatures.cones: Upright green-then-brown cones 10–15 cm that disintegrate on the tree, leaving a spike.
idFeatures.habit: Tall columnar montane fir; needles attached by a disk, not pegs.

species.biome: southern European montane and planted forest
species.nativeRange: Southern Europe, Turkey, northwest Africa; widely planted
species.whyCommon: A major southern European and plantation pine, among the most frequent pines on European plots after Scots pine.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray to blackish, thick and plated; no orange upper trunk like Scots pine.
idFeatures.needles: Two stiff, dark-green needles 8–16 cm, longer and less blue than Scots pine.
idFeatures.cones: Sessile, ovoid, yellow-brown cones 5–10 cm, unarmed or nearly so.
idFeatures.habit: Sturdy montane or plantation pine used in European afforestation.

species.nativeRange: Europe and western Asia
species.whyCommon: The typical large European riverside willow and a parent of cricket-bat and weeping cultivars; widespread along rivers.

idFeatures.bark: Deeply fissured gray-brown on old trunks; twigs often yellowish.
idFeatures.leaves: Long, narrow, finely toothed, silky-white beneath (hence white).
idFeatures.flowers: Dioecious catkins appearing with the leaves in spring.
idFeatures.habit: Large, often leaning riparian tree, frequently pollarded.

species.biome: temperate European forest and global urban canopy
species.nativeRange: Europe and western Asia; widely planted and invasive in North America
species.whyCommon: A common European forest maple and one of the world's most planted urban shade trees; a lookalike of sugar maple.

idFeatures.bark: Gray, remaining relatively smooth with interlacing grooves, not sugar maple's plated ridges.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, 5–7 sharply pointed lobes; milky sap in the petiole when snapped (key vs sugar maple).
idFeatures.fruit: Paired samaras almost 180 degrees apart, ripening in autumn.
idFeatures.habit: Dense urban shade tree; often purple-leaved cultivars.

species.biome: eastern US woodland; globally planted and invasive
species.nativeRange: Appalachian and Ozark US; naturalized worldwide
species.whyCommon: One of the most widely planted and naturalized temperate trees globally for erosion control, honey, and timber; frequent on European plots.

idFeatures.bark: Deeply furrowed, rope-like gray ridges.
idFeatures.leaves: Alternate, pinnately compound, 7–21 oval leaflets; paired stipular spines at nodes.
idFeatures.flowers: Hanging white, fragrant pea-flowers in late spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Flat brown legumes 5–10 cm.

species.biome: North American riparian and planted forest
species.nativeRange: Central and eastern North America
species.whyCommon: The giant floodplain poplar of the US interior and a parent of globally planted hybrid poplars used in short-rotation forestry.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth pale when young; old trunks deeply furrowed into thick gray ridges.
idFeatures.leaves: Deltoid (triangular) with a coarsely toothed margin and a flattened petiole; glands at the blade base.
idFeatures.flowers: Dioecious catkins; female trees release cottony seeds.
idFeatures.habit: Massive fast-growing riparian tree.

species.nativeRange: Garden hybrid of P. orientalis × P. occidentalis
species.whyCommon: The world's most planted large urban street tree; millions line cities from London to Beijing to New York.

idFeatures.bark: Camouflage bark peeling in large cream, olive, and brown plates.
idFeatures.leaves: Maple-like, palmately 3–5 lobed, but alternate (maples are opposite).
idFeatures.fruit: Bristly spherical multiple achenes, usually in pairs on a hanging stalk.
idFeatures.habit: Massive, pollution-tolerant street tree with a broad crown.

species.biome: Mediterranean and Atlantic coastal pine forest
species.nativeRange: Western Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts of SW Europe and NW Africa
species.whyCommon: A Mediterranean forestry dominant, among the most frequent pines on European plots; extensively planted for timber, resin, and dunes.

idFeatures.bark: Very thick, deeply fissured, reddish-brown to gray plates.
idFeatures.needles: Two very long, stiff, glossy needles 10–25 cm.
idFeatures.cones: Large, glossy, clustered cones 8–20 cm that may remain closed several years.
idFeatures.habit: Coastal and dune pine of the Landes, Iberia, and Maghreb.

species.nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin
species.whyCommon: The characteristic lowland pine of the Mediterranean, frequent on European plots and widely planted in dry climates.

idFeatures.bark: Orange-red and flaky on the upper trunk, gray-brown below.
idFeatures.needles: Two slender, pale-green needles 6–12 cm, more flexible than black pine.
idFeatures.cones: Reddish-brown cones 5–12 cm on thick recurved stalks, often remaining closed (serotinous).
idFeatures.habit: Open, irregular crown of dry hills and coasts.

species.nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin
species.whyCommon: The signature evergreen oak of Mediterranean woodlands (dehesa and maquis) and among the most frequent trees on southern European plots.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray, finely cracked into small plates; not corky.
idFeatures.leaves: Evergreen, leathery, holly-like to lanceolate, dark green above, densely gray-hairy below; juvenile leaves spiny.
idFeatures.fruit: Small pointed acorns one-third to one-half enclosed in a scaly cup.
idFeatures.habit: Dense, rounded evergreen crown; contrast cork oak's thick corky bark.

species.nativeRange: Western Mediterranean (Iberia, Maghreb, Sardinia, Corsica, Italy)
species.whyCommon: Economic and ecological dominant of Iberian montado/dehesa; the world's cork source and a widespread Mediterranean evergreen oak.

idFeatures.bark: Unmistakable thick, spongy, deeply furrowed cork; freshly stripped trunks are brick-red.
idFeatures.leaves: Evergreen, oval, wavy-toothed, gray-hairy below.
idFeatures.fruit: Acorns with a short-fringed cup, often in small clusters.
idFeatures.habit: Open-grown evergreen oak of grazed woodlands.

species.nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin and adjacent western Asia; planted worldwide in dry-summer climates
species.whyCommon: One of the most widely cultivated tree crops on Earth; millions of orchard trees define Mediterranean landscapes.

idFeatures.bark: Pale gray, gnarled, and deeply fissured on ancient trunks.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, lanceolate, leathery, gray-green above and silvery below.
idFeatures.flowers: Small creamy panicles in spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Drupe (olive) green then black, with a hard pit.

species.biome: Mediterranean coastal woodland and planted landscape
species.nativeRange: Mediterranean Basin
species.whyCommon: The umbrella pine of Mediterranean coasts and cities; widely planted and the source of pine nuts.

idFeatures.bark: Orange-brown, deeply plated into vertical fissures.
idFeatures.needles: Two stout, gray-green needles 10–20 cm.
idFeatures.cones: Massive globose cones 8–15 cm with thick scales; large wingless edible seeds (pine nuts).
idFeatures.habit: Unmistakable flat, umbrella-shaped crown on a tall clean bole.

species.biome: East Asian urban and temple landscapes; wild remnant in China
species.nativeRange: China (wild remnant populations debated); planted across East Asia and globally
species.whyCommon: A living fossil and one of East Asia's most planted urban trees; globally common in cities even though wild trees are rare.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, deeply furrowed into ridges on old trees.
idFeatures.leaves: Fan-shaped, often bilobed, with dichotomous veins and no midrib; gold in autumn.
idFeatures.fruit: Dioecious; female trees produce fleshy, foul-smelling yellow seeds (not a true fruit).
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled, often excurrent urban tree.

species.nativeRange: China and Taiwan; invasive on every inhabited continent
species.whyCommon: One of the most successful invasive urban trees worldwide; extremely abundant in cities and along transport corridors.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth pale gray with pale vertical streaks; not deeply furrowed until old.
idFeatures.leaves: Very large odd-pinnate leaves 30–90 cm; leaflets with a glandular tooth near the base and a rank peanut-butter odor when crushed.
idFeatures.flowers: Dioecious panicles; male flowers malodorous.
idFeatures.fruit: Twisted samaras in large hanging clusters, pink then brown.

species.nativeRange: Tropical and subtropical East and Southeast Asia to Australia; planted pantropically
species.whyCommon: One of the most planted tropical street and park figs from Hong Kong to Florida to the Mediterranean; a hyper-common urban tree of warm cities.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth pale gray; often with aerial roots on older trees.
idFeatures.leaves: Alternate, elliptic, glossy, with a short drip tip and a prominent pair of basal veins.
idFeatures.fruit: Small paired figs (syconia) in leaf axils, green then pink or black.
idFeatures.habit: Dense rounded crown; may form a banyan-like mass of aerial roots in humid climates.

species.nativeRange: South America (NW Argentina, Bolivia); planted worldwide in warm cities
species.whyCommon: One of the world's most planted ornamental street trees in frost-free cities (Pretoria, Brisbane, Los Angeles, Mexico City).

idFeatures.bark: Thin, gray-brown, finely fissured.
idFeatures.leaves: Bipinnate, fern-like, with many tiny leaflets.
idFeatures.flowers: Trumpet-shaped mauve-blue panicles covering the crown in spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Flat woody circular capsules.

species.nativeRange: Amazonia and adjacent tropical South America
species.whyCommon: Amazon hyperdominant: ter Steege et al. estimated about 5.2 billion stems, tied for the most abundant Amazonian tree.

idFeatures.bark: Slender, ringed, solitary gray stem (not clustering like E. oleracea).
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnate fronds in a spreading crown with a prominent green to yellow crownshaft.
idFeatures.fruit: Small purple-black drupes in hanging infructescences (açaí).
idFeatures.habit: Single-stemmed canopy palm of terra firme and floodplain; contrast clumping E. oleracea.

species.nativeRange: Amazonia and the Guiana Shield
species.whyCommon: The only Amazon hyperdominant ranked dominant in all six Amazonian regions; about 5.0 billion stems in ter Steege et al. 2013.

idFeatures.bark: Gray to brown, often flaking; typical of Brazil-nut relatives.
idFeatures.leaves: Simple, leathery, elliptic leaves with entire margins.
idFeatures.flowers: Cauliflorous to ramiflorous zygomorphic flowers with a coiled androecial hood (Lecythidaceae).
idFeatures.fruit: Woody pyxidia (pot-like capsules) that open by a lid, with winged seeds.

species.nativeRange: Central America to western Amazonia
species.whyCommon: Amazon hyperdominant with about 4.1 billion stems; a widespread stilt-rooted canopy palm.

idFeatures.bark: Tall gray stem with a characteristic barrel-like swelling above dense black stilt roots.
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnate fronds with praemorse (chopped-looking) leaflet tips.
idFeatures.fruit: Yellow-orange globose fruits in hanging clusters.
idFeatures.habit: Emergent palm with a swollen stem; stilt roots are the field mark.

species.nativeRange: Northern South America, especially the Amazon estuary
species.whyCommon: Amazon hyperdominant (about 3.8 billion stems) and a major fruit crop; the clumping açaí of várzea, a lookalike of solitary E. precatoria.

idFeatures.bark: Multiple slender ringed stems in a clump (the split from solitary E. precatoria).
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnate fronds with a green crownshaft.
idFeatures.fruit: Dense hanging bunches of small purple açaí drupes.
idFeatures.habit: Clumping floodplain and estuary palm, widely cultivated.

species.nativeRange: Amazon Basin; planted throughout the humid tropics
species.whyCommon: Amazon hyperdominant (about 1.9 billion wild stems) and a globally planted latex crop; FAO counted about 9.9 million ha of Hevea plantations around 2000.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth gray bark that weeps white latex from tapping cuts; plantation trunks are often spiral-scarred.
idFeatures.leaves: Trifoliate leaves with long petioles; leaflets elliptic with drip tips.
idFeatures.fruit: Three-lobed capsules that explode to eject seeds.
idFeatures.habit: Straight-boled canopy tree in plantations; wild trees are Amazon terra firme trees.

species.nativeRange: Central America and Amazonia
species.whyCommon: Amazon hyperdominant (about 2.7 billion stems); one of the most recognizable Neotropical palms.

idFeatures.bark: Slender stem raised on a cone of spiny stilt roots — the walking palm look.
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnate fronds with jagged leaflet tips.
idFeatures.fruit: Yellow-orange oval fruits.
idFeatures.habit: Subcanopy palm standing on an open stilt-root cone; contrast Iriartea's swollen stem.

species.biome: tropical rainforest and dry forest; also planted
species.nativeRange: Neotropics and tropical West Africa; planted pantropically
species.whyCommon: A widespread tropical emergent of both Amazonian and West African forests, and a planted village and fiber tree across the tropics.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-green, often with large conical spines on young trunks; huge buttresses on emergents.
idFeatures.leaves: Palmately compound with 5–9 leaflets.
idFeatures.flowers: Creamy-white nocturnal flowers before or with new leaves.
idFeatures.fruit: Large hanging capsules packed with silky kapok fiber and seeds.
idFeatures.habit: Umbrella-crowned emergent, among the largest tropical trees.

species.nativeRange: Peninsular Malaysia, Sumatra, Borneo
species.whyCommon: With R. parvifolia, among the most common and widespread emergents of lowland dipterocarp forest in Indonesia and Malaysia (formerly Shorea leprosula).

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, flaky; bole with buttresses.
idFeatures.leaves: Elliptic to ovate, undersides often coppery-scaly (leprosula = finely scaly).
idFeatures.fruit: Five-winged dipterocarp nut, three long wings and two short.
idFeatures.habit: Large light-red meranti of clayey to sandy lowland forest.

species.biome: South Asian tropical moist and dry deciduous forest
species.nativeRange: India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan; Himalayan foothills
species.whyCommon: India's most abundant forest tree, covering about 10 million ha (about 11% of Indian forest); also about 1 million ha in Nepal.

idFeatures.bark: Dark, thick, and fissured; coppices strongly after cutting or fire.
idFeatures.leaves: Large ovate-oblong leathery leaves with cordate bases, turning red before falling in the dry season.
idFeatures.flowers: Creamy-yellow panicles in spring.
idFeatures.fruit: Ovoid nut with five unequal wings.

species.nativeRange: India, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos; planted pantropically
species.whyCommon: The most widely planted high-value tropical hardwood; FAO reported about 2.3–5.7 million ha of teak plantations, mostly in Asia.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, peeling in long fibrous strips; sapwood pale, heartwood golden.
idFeatures.leaves: Very large, opposite, ovate, rough above and densely hairy below; 15–45 cm.
idFeatures.flowers: Large terminal panicles of small white flowers in the rainy season.
idFeatures.fruit: Inflated papery four-lobed drupe.

species.nativeRange: South and Southeast Asia; planted in tropics worldwide
species.whyCommon: A leading tropical plantation hardwood (FAO listed it among major industrial species with high MAI); widely planted in Asia, Africa, and Latin America.

idFeatures.bark: Pale gray-brown, smooth then flaking in patches.
idFeatures.leaves: Opposite, broadly ovate, 10–20 cm, with a cordate base and long petiole.
idFeatures.flowers: Yellow-brown tubular flowers in terminal panicles.
idFeatures.fruit: Yellow-orange drupes about 2 cm.

species.biome: South Asian riverine forest and plantation
species.nativeRange: Indian subcontinent; planted in Asia and Africa
species.whyCommon: Among the three most widely planted high-value tropical hardwoods; FAO reported about 626,000 ha, 95% in India and Pakistan.

idFeatures.bark: Gray-brown, longitudinally furrowed, peeling in strips.
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnately compound with 3–5 roundish leaflets, the terminal leaflet largest.
idFeatures.flowers: Pale yellow pea-flowers in axillary panicles.
idFeatures.fruit: Thin, flat, pale-brown pods with 1–4 seeds.

species.biome: South Asian dry forest and planted tropics
species.nativeRange: Indian subcontinent; planted across dry tropics of Africa and Asia
species.whyCommon: One of the most widely planted multipurpose trees of the dry tropics (shade, medicine, pesticide); a village and roadside tree from India to the Sahel.

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray, deeply fissured into plates.
idFeatures.leaves: Pinnate with many sickle-shaped, serrated leaflets; bitter when chewed.
idFeatures.flowers: Small white fragrant panicles.
idFeatures.fruit: Yellow-green olive-like drupes.

species.biome: tropical plantation and West African rainforest
species.nativeRange: West and southwest Africa; planted throughout the humid tropics
species.whyCommon: The fastest-expanding tree crop on Earth; about 20–29 million ha of plantations (FAO harvested area ~28.7 million ha by 2020), plus wild West African stands.

idFeatures.bark: Stout, solitary stem clothed in persistent woody leaf bases, becoming smoother and ringed with age.
idFeatures.leaves: Huge pinnate fronds 3–5 m with spines on the petiole.
idFeatures.fruit: Dense bunches of reddish plum-sized fruits (oily mesocarp plus a kernel).
idFeatures.habit: Stocky plantation palm to about 20 m; not to be confused with coconut's smooth gray stem and larger fruit.

species.nativeRange: Central Indo-Pacific; ubiquitous on tropical coasts
species.whyCommon: Pantropical coastal and village palm; FAO reported about 12 million ha of coconut plantations around 1997, plus countless trees outside forests.

idFeatures.bark: Tall, slender, smooth gray stem with even rings and a slight lean toward the light.
idFeatures.leaves: Very long pinnate fronds 4–6 m in a spreading crown; no crownshaft.
idFeatures.fruit: Large fibrous drupe (coconut) in clusters below the crown.
idFeatures.habit: Classic leaning beach palm; contrast oil palm's stout stem and dense red fruit bunches.

species.biome: tropical and subtropical plantation; native wet eucalypt forest
species.nativeRange: Eastern Australia; the most widely planted eucalypt worldwide
species.whyCommon: FAO called E. grandis the most widely planted Eucalyptus species; one of nine species that make up about 90% of >25 million ha of eucalypt plantations.

idFeatures.bark: Smooth, powdery white to blue-gray on the upper trunk; rough fibrous bark at the base.
idFeatures.leaves: Adult leaves lanceolate, glossy green, hanging; juvenile leaves opposite and ovate.
idFeatures.fruit: Pear-shaped woody capsules (gumnuts) with 4–5 valves.
idFeatures.habit: Very tall, straight plantation and wet-forest eucalypt.

species.nativeRange: Tasmania and southern Victoria; planted in Mediterranean climates worldwide
species.whyCommon: One of the nine eucalypts that dominate global plantations; historically the most-studied and widely planted eucalypt in cooler climates (Iberia, California, Andes, Ethiopia).

idFeatures.bark: Smooth, peeling in long ribbons to cream, gray, and bluish patches; rough at the very base.
idFeatures.leaves: Adult leaves long, sickle-shaped, glossy dark green, strongly aromatic; juvenile leaves opposite, glaucous, round.
idFeatures.fruit: Large warty, glaucous, top-shaped capsules with a thick rim — the diagnostic globulus gumnut.
idFeatures.habit: Tall aromatic eucalypt of cool-temperate plantations.

species.biome: Australian riparian woodland and dry-tropics plantation
species.nativeRange: Most of mainland Australia; planted in dry tropics worldwide
species.whyCommon: Australia's most widespread eucalypt and one of the most planted eucalypts in dry and semi-arid tropics (India, Pakistan, Africa, Mediterranean).

idFeatures.bark: Smooth, mottled cream, gray, and pale red, shedding in flakes; often stained.
idFeatures.leaves: Narrow, hanging, gray-green lanceolate leaves.
idFeatures.fruit: Small hemispherical capsules with strongly exserted valves.
idFeatures.habit: Spreading riparian tree, often with a massive leaning bole.

species.nativeRange: Tiny native range in California and Mexico; planted in NZ, Chile, Australia, Spain
species.whyCommon: The most widely planted introduced conifer, with just over 4 million ha (Chile, New Zealand, Australia hold >90%).

idFeatures.bark: Dark gray-brown, deeply fissured into thick ridges.
idFeatures.needles: Usually three bright-green needles 8–15 cm, slender and flexible.
idFeatures.cones: Asymmetric, ovoid, often clustered and serotinous cones 7–15 cm that persist for years.
idFeatures.habit: Fast-growing plantation pine of mild, moist temperate climates.

species.nativeRange: Caribbean, Bahamas, and Central America; planted in the tropics
species.whyCommon: A principal tropical plantation pine (with P. elliottii, P. oocarpa, P. patula) occupying a large share of the global fast-growing pine estate.

idFeatures.bark: Reddish-brown, plated, becoming thick and fissured.
idFeatures.needles: Usually three (sometimes two) slender needles 15–25 cm.
idFeatures.cones: Narrow conical cones 5–12 cm with small prickles.
idFeatures.habit: Tropical pine of savannas and plantations; more heat-tolerant than loblolly.

plates.commonsTitle: File:Pinus caribaea var bahamensis Lucayan National Park 3.jpg

species.nativeRange: Eastern Mexico; planted in African and Andean highlands
species.whyCommon: A leading tropical highland plantation pine (East Africa, southern Africa, Andes), grouped by FAO among the fast-growing pines that occupy about 25% of tropical-subtropical softwood plantings.

idFeatures.bark: Reddish-orange and flaky on the upper trunk; gray and plated below.
idFeatures.needles: Three (rarely four) very slender, drooping, bright-green needles 15–30 cm.
idFeatures.cones: Curved, clustered cones 7–12 cm, often remaining closed.
idFeatures.habit: Weeping-needled highland plantation pine.

plates.commonsTitle: File:Starr-040214-0061-Pinus patula-cones on dying tree-Puu Nianiau-Maui (24605036231).jpg

species.biome: East Asian temperate plantation and forest
species.nativeRange: Japan and southern China; Japan's dominant plantation tree
species.whyCommon: Sugi covers about 4.4 million ha, ~44% of Japan's plantation forest, making it one of the world's most planted single species.

idFeatures.bark: Reddish-brown, peeling in long vertical fibrous strips.
idFeatures.needles: Awl-shaped, spirally arranged, incurved needles 0.5–1.5 cm clothing the shoots.
idFeatures.cones: Small globose cones 1.5–3 cm with pointed scale tips.
idFeatures.habit: Straight, columnar plantation tree; Japan's signature timber species (sugi).
